summary: Describes the EPP mapping for managing contact identifiers, the records for people or organizations tied to registry objects. It defines EPP command syntax and meaning for contacts, in XML. It was replaced by RFC 4933.

eli5.summary: Every web address has someone responsible for it. This part of the registry language handles the records of who those people are.

subtitle: How to manage contact information for domain registry objects in EPP.

tldr.problem: Domain registries need a standardized way to store and manage contact information for individuals and organizations associated with registered domains and other registry objects.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the EPP contact mapping, allowing registrars to create, query, transfer, and update contact records using standardized XML commands, with support for internationalized names and privacy preferences.
tldr.outcome: Registries can maintain contact information consistently while respecting privacy choices and authorization controls. RFC 4933 updated this specification.

today: RFC 4933 updated this specification in May 2007 with enhancements to the EPP contact mapping.

sections.title: Introduction and Contact Objects
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, defined in RFC 3730) is the standard protocol for provisioning objects in domain registries. This document describes the EPP mapping for contact objects—records that identify individuals or organizations associated with registry objects like domains, hosts, or other provisioned entities.

A contact object stores personal or organizational information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and authorization credentials. Contacts can be linked to multiple registry objects and can be transferred between registrar clients. The RFC supports both internationalized (ASCII-compatible) and localized (full UTF-8) versions of names and addresses to accommodate worldwide registrants.
sections.eli5: The registry keeps track of who owns or manages each domain. It stores their name, address, phone, and email. This describes how to add and change those records in the registry.

sections.title: Contact Attributes and Information
sections.content:
Every EPP contact object stores:

  • Contact identifier: A server-unique ID assigned by the registry when the contact is created.
  • Names: Individual name and optional organization name, available in both internationalized (7-bit ASCII) and localized (full UTF-8) forms.
  • Postal address: Street address (up to three lines), city, state or province, postal code, and country code (using ISO 3166 two-character codes).
  • Telephone numbers: Voice phone and optional fax number, following the E.164 international format (starting with + and country code).
  • Email address: Contact email as defined in RFC 2822.
  • Authorization information: Password-based credentials used to prove ownership during transfers and queries.
  • Status values: Flags like ok (normal), linked (in use by other objects), or clientDeleteProhibited (cannot be deleted).
  • Dates: Creation date, last update date, and last transfer date.
  • Disclosure preferences: Settings to control which contact attributes can be publicly disclosed, respecting privacy laws and client preferences.
sections.eli5: The contact record stores a name, address, phone, email, and a password. It also tracks who can see what information and whether the contact is locked from changes.

sections.title: EPP Operations on Contacts
sections.content:
EPP provides several commands to manage contact objects:

Query commands: The <check> command tests if a contact ID is available for creation. The <info> command retrieves all details about a contact, including postal address, phone numbers, status, and dates. The <transfer> query command allows a client to check the status of a pending contact transfer.

Transform commands: The <create> command creates a new contact with a chosen ID, name, address, phone, email, authorization password, and optional disclosure preferences. The <delete> command removes a contact if it is not associated with other objects. The <transfer> command initiates a sponsorship change (moving the contact to a different registrar). The <update> command modifies contact attributes: it can add or remove status values, or change address, phone, email, or authorization information.

All commands use XML format and follow the standard EPP envelope structure. Servers can defer transform commands for human review, returning a pending status until the action is approved.
sections.eli5: You can check if a contact ID exists, create a new contact, get its details, change it, transfer it to another registrar, or delete it.

sections.title: Contact Transfers and Privacy Controls
sections.content:
Contact transfers: A contact can be transferred from one registrar client to another using the <transfer> command. The losing registrar receives a transfer request; the gaining registrar must approve it (or both can approve or reject the transfer). Authorization information (the contact password) can be used to prove ownership. Transfer operations include status tracking: pending (awaiting action), approved, rejected, or cancelled. Once transferred, the new client becomes the sponsor of the contact.

Privacy and disclosure: Contacts have optional disclosure preferences that let clients indicate which contact details should be withheld from public WHOIS queries or directory listings. The client can set a disclosure flag to either allow or restrict disclosure of specific fields: name, organization, address, phone, fax, or email. Disclosure preferences are subject to the registry's data collection and publication policies; servers must reject preferences that violate their policies.

Only the sponsoring client can see the full contact information, including authorization details. Unauthorized clients see only what the disclosure preferences permit.
sections.eli5: Contacts can be moved from one registrar to another like a domain transfer. You can choose to keep your phone number and email private if you want—the registry respects your privacy choices.
